overview.text: The mole (symbol mol) is the SI base unit for amount of substance—a way to express how many specified microscopic entities a sample contains, rather than its mass. One mole is defined as exactly 6.02214076 × 10^23 entities, the fixed numerical value of the Avogadro constant. The entities must be identified, such as atoms, molecules, ions, or electrons. This makes the mole a chemical counting unit: it helps connect particle-level formulas and reactions to measurable samples. A mole does not have one fixed mass; equal amounts of different substances weigh differently because their particles have different masses. Since 2019, its definition fixes a number directly rather than relying on the mass of carbon-12.

key_facts.text: The unit symbol is mol; the symbol for amount of substance is n.
The counted entities must be specified and can include atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, or groups of particles.
The Avogadro constant is exactly 6.02214076 × 10^23 mol⁻¹; this is the number of entities in one mole.
A mole counts entities, not a fixed mass: one mole of different substances can have different masses.
The current definition took effect in 2019; the earlier definition linked the mole to the number of atoms in 12 grams of carbon-12.
